data.title: Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication
data.summary: Authentication endpoints accepted unlimited attempts, so passwords could be guessed at speed and credentials leaked elsewhere could be tested against every account in bulk.
data.description:
Credential stuffing is the dominant route into accounts, and it depends entirely on being able to make many attempts cheaply. Attackers replay username and password pairs from public breach corpora; because password reuse is common, a small success rate across a large list still yields valid sessions.

Unthrottled endpoints also allow password spraying — one common password against every account — which evades per-account lockout while remaining effective against any population with weak passwords.

The same gap applies to the endpoints around authentication: one-time-code verification, password reset, and registration, which additionally allows user enumeration at scale.
data.recommendation:
* Rate limit by account and by source address, with increasing delays, across login, reset, registration and code verification.
* Lock or step up verification after repeated failures, preferring a temporary lock with notification over a permanent one.
* Deploy multi-factor authentication; it is the control that makes stuffing uneconomic.
* Check new and changed passwords against a breached-password corpus.
* Alert on bulk failures and on successful logins following a burst of failures.
data.short_recommendation: Rate limit and lock out by account and by source.
